overview.text: Muhammad (c. 570–632) was an Arabian religious and community leader whose preaching in Mecca in the early seventh century became the beginning of Islam. Muslims believe God revealed the Qur’an to him through the angel Gabriel; in Islamic belief, he is the final prophet in a line that includes Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. His message called people to worship one God. In 622, he and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina in the hijra, where he helped establish a Muslim community; the migration marks the start of the Islamic calendar. Muslims also look to his reported words and actions, preserved in hadith and sunnah, as guidance alongside the Qur’an. Historical details in later biographies are not all equally certain.

key_facts.text: The broad traditional chronology places Muhammad’s birth in Mecca around 570 and his death in Medina in 632.
Muslims believe the Qur’an consists of revelations given to Muhammad by God through the angel Gabriel.
The hijra, Muhammad and his followers’ migration from Mecca to Medina in 622, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.
The Qur’an is Islam’s sacred text, but it is not a continuous narrative biography of Muhammad.
Hadith reports preserve accounts of Muhammad’s words and actions; his sunnah, or example, is important in Muslim religious life.
